title: Neural TTS: A Voice That Doesn't Sound Like a Robot | vitalii.no
description:
How five to ten videos a day got a human-sounding narrator for a few dollars instead of two thousand.

Producing five to ten videos a day meant every one of them needed a voice. Standard text-to-speech from Google or AWS Polly sounded painfully robotic and made the content feel cheap. Hiring real voiceover artists cost 50 to 200 dollars per video, which works out at 250 to 2000 dollars a day. Neither option was survivable.

The generateVideoScript service now sends raw text to the Zvukogram API, a deliberate pivot away from OpenAI TTS chosen for better voice quality and far more accurate timestamps. The API returns an mp3 file alongside a JSON payload of word_timestamps, an array of word, start_time and end_time objects. That data feeds Remotion's AnimatedSubtitles component directly, so every spoken word is highlighted at the exact moment it is said.

Voiceover quality is now hard to tell apart from a human narrator, and daily spend fell from 250-2000 dollars to a handful. The word-level sync turned generic captions into a polished overlay that measurably improves engagement and accessibility.
